# Context and motivation {background-color="#491106ff"}

## Background

::: {.box-inv-4 .sp-after .fragment style="font-size: 110%;"}

1) Privatization and marketization of public goods, welfare policies, and social services [@gingrich_making_2011; @streeck_how_2016]

:::

::: {.box-inv-4 .sp-after .fragment style="font-size: 110%;"}

2) Changes in the institutional architecture of the welfare state; expansion of market logics [@ferre_welfare_2023; @busemeyer_welfare_2020]

:::

::: {.box-inv-4 .sp-after .fragment style="font-size: 110%;"}

3) This economic order is reflected in a specific moral economy and policy feedback dynamics [@mau_inequality_2015; @campbell_institutional_2020; @fernandez_positive_2013]

:::

::: {.box-inv-5 .sp-after-half .fragment style="font-size: 110%;"}

Market justice preferences [@busemeyer_skills_2015; @castillo_perceptions_2025; @koos_moral_2019; @lindh_public_2015]

:::


::: {.notes}
Estados de bienestar que han expandido las lógicas de mercado vía privatización y mercantilización de bienes públicos, políticas y servicios sociales. Esto tiene consecuencias distributivas y también morales. Ese orden económico se refleja en una economía moral específica y en dinámicas de policy feedback: las instituciones incrustan criterios de mercado de asignación "justa" y reconfiguran el merecimiento y el balance Estado–mercado. En ese contexto crecen las market justice preferences: en qué medida la ciudadanía ve los criterios de mercado como base justa para asignar servicios esenciales —salud, educación, pensiones.
:::


## The problem


:::: {.incremental style="font-size: 120%;"}

- Deservingness back on top: *who should get what, and why?* —>  contributive / ability-to-pay welfare logic [@vanoorschot_social_2017]

- A key explanatory variable of this puzzle is meritocratic beliefs:

  → Stronger meritocratic perceptions lead to more MJP across pensions, education, and healthcare in Chile [@castillo_perceptions_2025; @castillo_justification_2026]

- **Aim**: examine in depth how the distinct dimensions of meritocracy drive more or less support for market-based welfare 

::::


## Multidimensional framework of meritocracy

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Castillo et al. (2023) measurement model"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: '100%'
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
library(knitr)
library(here)

knitr::include_graphics("images/diagramas(4).png")

```

:::

::: {.notes}

To approach meritocracy, we use a multidimensional framework. This model expands the usual way meritocracy is measured in empirical research [@castillo_multidimensional_2023].

:::
## Multidimensional framework of meritocracy



```{r}
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-cap: "Castillo et al. (2023) measurement model"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: '100%'


knitr::include_graphics("images/diagramas(5).png")

```

::: {.notes}

Most studies focus only on meritocratic perceptions, that is, whether people believe that effort and ability are actually rewarded in society. This is represented in the upper-left corner of the diagram. 

 

:::

## Multidimensional framework of meritocracy


```{r}
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-cap: "Castillo et al. (2023) measurement model"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: '100%'


knitr::include_graphics("images/diagramas(6).png")
```

::: {.notes}

What this model adds is, first, a distinction between perceptions and preferences, where perceptions refer to how people think society works and preferences refer to how they think it should work. This is represented in the upper-right corner using the same items, but with a normative sense. 


:::

## Multidimensional framework of meritocracy


```{r}
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-cap: "Castillo et al. (2023) measurement model"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: '100%'


knitr::include_graphics("images/diagramas(7).png")
```


::: {.notes}

Second, it also incorporates non-meritocratic elements, captured through items on family wealth and social connections, both of which are shown at the bottom of the diagram. We call this dimension non-meritocratic privilege.

:::

## Multidimensional framework of meritocracy


```{r}
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-cap: "Castillo et al. (2023) measurement model"
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: '100%'


knitr::include_graphics("images/diagramas(8).png")
```

::: {.notes}
So, in total, the scale distinguishes four dimensions: perceived meritocracy, perceived non-meritocracy, preference for meritocracy, and preference for non-meritocracy. This means that recognizing privilege does not oppose supporting merit. Both can coexist within the same belief system in terms of perceptions and preferences.


Also, you can see the two items for each factor, all measured on a four-point agreement scale.

:::

:::: {.fragment style="font-size: 110%;"}

**RQ:** How do meritocratic and privilege perceptions and preferences shape support for market-based welfare (health, education, pensions) in Chile?
